entries.subject: Ortiz et al. (2017) occultation and lightcurve ellipsoid
entries.finding: The body uses the nominal solution's semiaxes of 1,161 × 852 × 513 km with the preferred pole at J2000 right ascension 285.1° and declination -10.6°; the README states this is an inferred shape, not a resolved mesh or a unique interior model.

entries.subject: Ortiz et al. (2017) equatorial ring geometry
entries.finding: The equatorial ring uses the same publication's 2,287 km radius and 70 km width; its gray and fixed opacity are schematic, it has no invented bands, it stays evenly lit and it uses no separate Shadows control.

entries.subject: Shared neutral gray for the unresolved surface
entries.finding: Preparation fills the shared projective surface atlas with the neutral gray (#808080 sRGB) and samples no model texture; the README calls the gray a display convention and claims no terrain, texture or map.

entries.subject: Retained JPL physical-primary state 920136108 at JD 2461286.5 TT
entries.finding: The prepared orbital position and conic use the pinned primary vector and validated epoch record shared with Hi'iaka, which replaced the older heliocentric conic in the prepared scene; the README says this is not a new long-term ephemeris.

entries.subject: Disagreeing middle-axis uncertainty in Ortiz et al. (2017)
entries.finding: The README records that the paper's main text and Methods give different uncertainties for the middle axis, 4 km and 2 km, while the nominal value agrees, so the adopted semiaxis is used with an unsettled error.
entries.revisitWhen: An erratum or a later publication settles the middle-axis uncertainty.

entries.subject: Absolute rotational orientation at the scene epoch
entries.finding: Known problems state that the pole is observationally constrained but the display meridian is arbitrary, because the measured 3.915341-hour period does not establish an absolute orientation at the application epoch; no fictitious rotational ephemeris is animated.
entries.revisitWhen: A published longitude system or absolute rotational ephemeris fixes Haumea's meridian at a known epoch.
